column4: The section links parents, birth, and the mother's bodily labor; this ayah joins kindness to parents with carrying and delivering a child in hardship, then names the period of pregnancy and weaning.

The source section begins with walid (parent) and walada (to give birth); here the mother carries her child through weakness upon weakness and nurses him, grounding the parent-child bond in bodily cost.
The section turns the womb's kinship into mercy between generations; the prayer asks God to show parents mercy as they raised the speaker when small.
This ayah puts al-arham (kinship ties) beside raqiban (a watcher), exactly the womb-to-relatives and raqaba-to-oversight branches the section develops.
The section traces birth's threatened interruption and asks for a community bound by mercy; this ayah names cutting al-arham (womb ties) as social corruption.
The section's near orphan and dust-covered poor reappear in the giving order: parents, near kin, orphans, and the needy receive wealth.
This ayah gathers parents, kin, orphan, poor, near neighbor, and companion by one's side, then condemns the boastful; it directly mirrors the section's circle of care and its rich boaster's opposite.
Here yatim (orphan), dhā qurba (near kin), and waṣṣākum (He enjoined you) meet in one command, as in the section's linked image of kinship, orphan care, and mutual counsel.
The section explicitly asks whether wealth and children bind people to God; this ayah says amwāl (wealth) and awlād (children) do not bring nearness, while faith and good action do.
The section develops tawāṣaw as joining people through connected counsel; this ayah repeats tawāṣaw for truth and patience, the very communal practice named in 90:17.
The section joins plant growth to people who show mercy among themselves; this ayah calls believers merciful among themselves and likens their mutual strengthening to a crop sending out a shoot.
The section's dictionary form tirb means a peer who grows alongside you; this ayah uses atrāban for equal-aged companions, giving the orphan's lost companionship a restored form.
The section explicitly connects q-r-b, nearness, with those drawn near to God; this ayah names them al-muqarrabūn.
After asking about orphans, the ayah says that mixing lives with theirs makes them your brothers; it reverses the section's orphan as lineage cut off into chosen kinship.
This account of righteousness combines kin, orphan, needy, freeing a neck (fī al-riqāb), and patience, closely joining the section's bodily and communal scenes.
The covenantal command groups kindness to parents, relatives, orphans, and needy people, the same move from descent to wider care that the section traces.
The source section says waṣiyya (bequest, from root w-ṣ-y) is speech joined across people; this ayah directs a bequest to parents and near kin at death.
The section's counsel-as-connection has a generational form here: Abraham and Jacob transmit their faith to their sons through waṣṣā, a testament.
The sons answer their father's deathbed question by naming the God of their fathers; this neighbor completes 2:132's transmission of faith down the family line.
This ayah makes the child's nursing a shared parental responsibility, requires mutual consent and consultation, and forbids harming a mother through her child.
The command to return orphans' property and not consume it joins the section's fatherless child to concrete protection by the surrounding community.
The ayah specifically warns guardians about justice to orphan girls, extending the section's orphan image to vulnerable kin whose care is entrusted to others.
Orphans are to be tested until marriageable and then given their property; this follows the section's severed lineage into protection as a child grows up.
The ayah assigns inheritance shares to men and women from parents and near kin, tying succession after death to the section's line of offspring and relatives.
At inheritance division, relatives, orphans, and needy people who are present must receive provision; the estate becomes a means of care for the section's vulnerable figures.
The warning to fear leaving weak offspring and to speak rightly connects adult decisions to the children who may be left without protection.
Consuming orphan property is described as eating fire; this is the sharp opposite of the section's feeding and mercy toward the orphan.
The ayah specifies children and parents as heirs, making the section's continuing lineage concrete in the distribution of a parent's estate.
This inheritance law names spouses, children, and siblings; it shows family ties persisting as claims after death, as the section's lineage image implies.
The prohibited kin categories include mothers who bore you and sisters through nursing; the ayah grounds family closeness in birth and shared nurture.
For accidental killing, this ayah requires freeing a believing neck and compensation to the victim's family unless waived; it links release, severed life, kin, and mercy.
Among the expiations for broken oaths are feeding needy people or freeing a neck, repeating the section's concrete acts of relief.
The share of public spoils is assigned to the Messenger, near kin, orphans, needy, and travelers, linking kin descent to provision for the vulnerable.
Zakat recipients include the poor, needy, and those in the necks (fī al-riqāb); the ayah gathers the section's poverty and emancipation images.
The section defines mutual counsel as joining one thing to another; this ayah praises those who join what God commanded to be joined, including kin ties.
This neighbor adds the section's patience and giving: those who join bonds endure patiently, pray, spend from provision, and repel evil with good.
The joining culminates in the presence of righteous parents, spouses, and descendants together in the Garden, completing the family and communal bond of 13:21.
Abraham asks for a secure town and protection for himself and his sons, joining residence, safety, and descendants as the section does through city, family, and faith.
Abraham settles some of his offspring in the uncultivated valley by the Sacred House and asks that hearts incline to them and provision come; lineage and place become a community.
The ayah names spouses, children, and grandchildren as God's provision, a direct statement of the lineage continuing from the section's walid and walad.
People emerge from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then receive hearing, sight, and hearts; birth opens into dependence and responsibility.
God commands giving to relatives, directly extending the section's qarāba (kinship) from a dictionary sense into a Qur'anic duty.
The command to give the relative, poor person, and traveler their due makes the section's near kin and dust-covered poor recipients of actual provision.
The command not to approach an orphan's property until maturity protects the fatherless child through the period when the section's lineage would otherwise be interrupted.
Zechariah fears that his family line will have no successor and asks for an heir; this is the section's concern with descendants who remain after a man.
The requested son is to inherit Zechariah and the family of Jacob; this neighbor specifies the successor relation behind the preceding plea.
The answer is the promised Yahya, a child born despite the parents' circumstances, completing the successor prayer in 19:5-6.
Zechariah names his old age and his wife's barrenness; the ayah makes the threatened birth and succession explicit.
God answers that creating Yahya is easy; the sign completes the reversal of the barrenness described in 19:8.
Mary conceives and withdraws with the child, extending the section's lineage image to a solitary pregnancy.
Mary's labor pains bring her to a palm trunk; this is a direct bodily scene of imminent delivery.
The voice beneath Mary reassures her during labor and points to a stream, completing the birth scene of 19:23 with relief.
The instruction to shake the palm so fresh dates fall gives Mary food immediately after labor, a concrete provision around childbirth.
Mary is told to eat, drink, and be comforted after birth; this completes the bodily and emotional care around the delivery.
Zechariah asks not to be left without an heir; the section's dictionary sense of a successor who remains after a man is stated as a prayer.
God responds by granting Yahya and making Zechariah's wife fit for childbirth, reversing the childlessness that threatened the line in 21:89.
The ayah describes creation from drop to clot to formed or unformed lump, placement in wombs, and emergence as infants: a full bodily arc behind the section's birth image.
Humanity's creation begins from an extract of clay, carrying the section's parent-and-child image back to the origin of human bodies.
The drop is placed in a secure resting place; this gives the section's womb-as-house-and-vessel an exact Qur'anic scene.
The successive clot, lump, bones, and flesh make the section's otherwise hidden formation in the womb visible.
Humanity is made from water and given blood kinship and marriage ties; this directly joins bodily origin to the social bonds the section traces.
The prayer for spouses and offspring who are a comfort to the eyes presents family closeness as a desired good, echoing the section's companion and descendant images.
The command to warn one's nearest kin takes qarāba as a concrete circle of address, matching the section's movement from close family outward.
The command to treat parents well is bounded when they press their child toward idolatry; the family tie remains, but faith sets a limit, as in the section's turn from lineage to belief.
The section's dictionary sense of miskin uses the root s-k-n for what the heart settles toward; here spouses are made so each may find repose in the other, alongside affection and mercy.
The command to give relatives, the needy, and the traveler their due is the ethical form of the section's closeness and care.
Even when parents urge idolatry, the child must not obey, yet must accompany them kindly; it marks faith as the boundary of descent while preserving mercy.
God alone knows what is in wombs; the ayah makes explicit the hidden pregnancy behind the section's visible signs of approaching birth.
The ayah says adopted sons are not one's actual sons, distinguishing social naming from the descent through a womb that the section develops.
Children are to be called by their fathers, which makes the section's father-based lineage explicit as a recognized tie.
The ayah says blood relatives are closer to one another than other believers, setting inherited kinship beside the faith-based community of the section.
The deniers claim that greater wealth and children protect them; this is the precise boast the section rebukes through its rich spender and its warning that offspring do not bring nearness.
The next ayah says provision expands or contracts by God's will, completing the reply to the wealthy people's claim in 34:35.
People are created from dust and then a drop, and females carry and deliver only with God's knowledge; this joins dust, descent, and pregnancy in one ayah.
Abraham asks for a righteous child, directly voicing the desire for lineage to continue.
The answer announces a forbearing boy, completing Abraham's prayer for offspring in 37:100.
The son has grown to work alongside his father; this is the section's dictionary branch of the son who becomes his father's companion.
Father and son submit together to the commanded sacrifice, bringing the threatened severing of descent into the very scene of their companionship.
A great ransom replaces the son; this neighbor completes the threatened lineage break with deliverance.
After Noah's deliverance, his offspring are made the survivors; the ayah states lineage continuing beyond the father.
God creates people in their mothers' wombs through successive formations in three darknesses, a direct image of the body's hidden preparation for birth.
The ayah follows a human from dust through a drop and clot to infant, adulthood, and old age, linking birth to the full lineage-bearing life.
God gives daughters or sons as offspring, making descent a gift rather than a human guarantee.
God may give both sexes or make whom He wills barren, a direct boundary on the lineage continuation named in the section.
Abraham's declaration is made a lasting word among his descendants; this directly joins counsel and belief across generations.
Believing descendants are joined to their parents in the Garden; lineage is preserved through faith, matching the section's shift from birth to a believing community.
The ayah says wives are not mothers except those who gave birth to them; it makes actual birth the boundary of the section's womb-based kinship.
For the false mother-claim, the expiation is freeing a neck; the ayah connects ruptured kinship language to the section's liberation of a raqaba.
If a neck cannot be freed, the next expiation is fasting or feeding sixty needy people; this neighbor completes 58:3 by moving from release to feeding.
The righteous feed the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for the food, bringing the section's three vulnerable figures into one act of mercy.
The word atrāban repeats the Qur'anic peer sense of the section's dictionary form tirb, here describing companions of equal age.
The section names those brought near as a form of q-r-b; this ayah uses al-muqarrabūn for those who witness the record of the righteous.
The same near ones drink from the sealed spring; it repeats the section's q-r-b link between closeness and a valued company.
The Lord is described as watching over people, completing the warning about oversight before the next passage tests how wealth treats orphan and poor.
The wealthy person assumes abundance means honor; this sets up the section's challenge to the man who boasts of spending heaps.
The person whose provision is narrowed assumes God has humiliated him; this contrasts worldly measurement with the section's care for the poor.
The passage says they do not honor the orphan, directly reversing the section's command to aid the fatherless child.
They do not urge one another to feed the poor, the exact social failure opposed by the section's feeding and mutual counsel.
They consume inheritance greedily; this reverses the section's concern for descendants and relatives left after a death.
They love wealth intensely, the opposite of turning wealth toward the orphan and destitute in the section.
God found the Prophet an orphan and sheltered him; the ayah makes the orphan's threatened isolation a scene of received protection.
The instruction not to oppress an orphan turns the Prophet's own orphanhood into a duty of care.
The asker must not be repelled; it extends the section's mercy from orphan to another person in need.
The section names insan and mutual counsel; this preceding ayah declares humankind in loss, which 103:3 then qualifies by faith, good works, truth, and patience.
The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and gives safety from fear, matching the section's hard day of hunger and faith as fear's removal.
The one who denies judgment is identified through how he treats the orphan, connecting belief to the section's measure of mercy.
The denier pushes away the orphan, a direct reversal of the section's aid to the fatherless.
He does not urge feeding the poor, the opposite of the section's feeding and mutual exhortation.
God forms people in wombs as He wills; this supplies a direct but general parallel to the section's hidden completion of the child before birth.
Zechariah asks God for good offspring, repeating the section's concern with descendants as a gift.
The angel announces Yahya, completing Zechariah's prayer for offspring in 3:38.
Zechariah names old age and his wife's barrenness; the promised birth overturns the section's dictionary image of a woman whose children do not survive.
The spouses seek repose in one another (root s-k-n), while the woman carries a light burden that grows heavy; this joins the section's miskin root and pregnancy image.
Believers are told not to take fathers and brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief; blood ties have a faith boundary, like the section's turn from descent to belief.
Believing men and women are allies of one another and command good; it gives the section's connected, merciful community a wider social form.
The ayah bars prayer for forgiveness for even close polytheist kin; it makes faith a specific boundary within the section's kinship bond.
Sarah receives the announcement of Isaac despite her age, a birth reversal of the section's lexicon for a woman without living children.
Sarah names herself an old barren woman; this completes the childbirth surprise begun in 11:71.
The visitors answer with God's decree and mercy, completing the announcement to the parents in 11:71-72.
God knows what each female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, a direct formulation of the section's hidden pregnancy and approaching birth.
Abraham asks how a child can be announced to him in old age, a direct birth reversal of childlessness.
The angels reaffirm the good news, completing Abraham's question about the announced child.
Abraham says only the astray despair of God's mercy; this neighbor completes the promise to elderly parents with the section's mercy theme.
The ayah names kin, poor, and emigrants while urging pardon and continued giving; it turns closeness into mercy toward vulnerable people.
The section's insan dictionary branch is familiarity without estrangement; here tasta'nisū means seeking familiarity before entering another household, beside greeting its people.
This neighbor sets the boundary for the household visit in 24:27: if no one is there, do not enter without permission.
Pharaoh offers the successful magicians a place among the muqarrabīn; nearness is presented as worldly favor, unlike the section's faith-shaped nearness to God.
God made the sanctuary secure while people around it were seized; this connects the section's town and neighbor image to safety within a shared place.
The section's dictionary branch of uns is familiarity; this ayah uses musta'nisīn for guests lingering in conversation and sets a boundary for entering the Prophet's household.
The word atrāb again means peers of equal age, preserving the section's secondary tirb sense in another Qur'anic description of company.
The disbelievers claim their idols bring them closer to God; this contrasts the section's true closeness through faith and compassionate action with a false means of approach.
Repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into an intimate friend; this is a specific reversal from separation to the section's joined community.
The next ayah says this change is granted to the patient, completing the enemy-to-friend reversal with the section's counsel to patience.
The ayah names affection toward near kin as a requested reward; the referent of the phrase is debated, but its kinship link is explicit.
Believers are called brothers and told to reconcile; it states the section's movement from isolated people to a bound community.
Humanity is made peoples and tribes to know one another, while honor is measured by piety; descent becomes a path to recognition rather than rank.
The ayah says God is nearer than the jugular vein; it gives the section's q-r-b theme a bodily image while making nearness more than human kinship.
The righteous keep a known right in their wealth for the asker and deprived, making the section's care for the poor a recurring social obligation.
The visitors give Abraham news of a knowledgeable son, repeating the unexpected birth that answers a childless household.
Sarah calls herself an old barren woman; the promised child reverses the section's image of a woman whose child does not live.
The visitors confirm that God has decreed the birth, completing Sarah's question in 51:29.
The ayah says God creates the two sexes, male and female, a direct account of the offspring arising from the section's birth image.
The creation of male and female is traced to an emitted drop, specifying the origin behind 53:45.
When the dying person is among those brought near, the ayah names rest, provision, and a garden; it extends the section's q-r-b link to a final welcome.
Kindness and justice are permitted toward those who did not fight or expel the believers, extending the section's mercy beyond inherited kin.
Spouses and children can become enemies, yet pardon and forgiveness are urged; family closeness is not automatic, and mercy repairs it.
The condemned person did not urge feeding the needy, the direct opposite of the section's feeding on a day of hunger and mutual counsel.
The righteous reserve a fixed right in their wealth, introducing the next ayah's asker and deprived as recipients of the section's care.
The next ayah names the asker and deprived as holders of that right, specifying the needy person in the section.
The man God created alone is given wealth and sons; the ayah joins solitude and lineage to a self-satisfied figure like the section's boaster.
The same man has sons at hand, making worldly lineage one of his sources of pride.
His wealth and status are expanded further, completing the description of the man with sons in 74:13.
He still wants more, showing that wealth and descendants do not end self-sufficiency, the stance challenged by the section.
The section ends with aṣḥāb al-maymana, companions of the right; this ayah uses the same companion term for those who escape the Fire.
The question about what brought people to Saqar begins a passage that identifies failure to pray and feed the needy, the section's contrary path.
The condemned say they were not among those who prayed; this is the first failure in the sequence opposing the section's right-hand community.
They say they did not feed the needy, directly reversing the section's relief for the poor.
They joined those who indulged in vain talk, the contrary social company completing the feeding failure in 74:44.
They denied the Day of Judgment; this completes the answer to 74:42 and links the abandoned poor to moral accountability.
The human begins as an emitted drop, directly connecting the section's offspring to bodily origin.
The drop becomes a clinging clot and is formed, specifying the next stage of 75:37.
The formed human is made male and female, completing the reproductive sequence begun in 75:37.
Humanity is created from a lowly fluid, a direct bodily origin for the section's descendants.
The fluid is placed in a secure resting place, echoing the section's womb as a vessel.
The placement lasts to a known term, giving the section's nearing birth a stated duration.
God measures the term, completing the pregnancy sequence of 77:20-22.
The buried girl is asked for what sin she was killed; this is a stark reversal of lineage surviving through birth and of the child whose life does not continue.
The next ayah says the buried girl was killed; it completes the violated birth and survival implied in 81:8.
The human is told to consider what he was created from, turning attention to the body's origin as the section does through birth and descent.
The origin is an emitted fluid, specifying the question in 86:5.
The fluid's bodily source is named, completing the reproductive origin described in 86:6.
The ayah says the human was created from a clot, a direct formation-in-the-womb image behind the section's birth arc.
The human transgresses when he sees himself self-sufficient, a precise counterpart to the section's boastful spender who imagines no one sees him.
The self-sufficient person forgets dependence; the section's faith and mercy answer this posture with mutual obligation.
The wealth collector thinks his property will make him last forever, a specific contrast to the section's lineage and communal care.
The next ayah says he will be thrown into the Crusher, completing the false security attached to wealth in 104:2.
The rich garden-owner boasts of wealth and children; his ṣāḥib (companion) answers him, contrasting the section's boastful man with a companion who counsels him.
The wealthy man enters his garden wronging himself, turning the section's connected plant image into private possession and self-regard.
He doubts the Hour and assumes his garden will endure, the opposite of the section's dependence on faith, patience, and care for vulnerable people.
His companion answers that God created him from dust and then a drop; birth and companionship challenge wealth as the measure of a person.
The garden's fruit is ruined and its owner wrings his hands, reversing the section's plant growth and the boast that possessions endure.
He has no group to help him against God, the isolated end of a man whose section-like wealth and descendants did not make a merciful community.
Protection and true authority belong to God, completing the garden owner's loss of human support in 18:43.
Qarun is arrogant among his people because of vast wealth, a specific contrast to the section's generosity toward the poor.
His people tell him to do good as God has done good to him and not seek corruption; this states the social use of wealth that the section asks for.
Qarun claims his wealth came from his own knowledge, opposing the section's account of human dependence and mutual care.
Qarun and his house are swallowed and no group can help him; wealth and household fail to provide the companionship the section values.
The onlookers learn that provision is not proof of favor, completing Qarun's fall and the section's challenge to wealth-based honor.
The ayah asks whether deniers across generations advised one another to reject truth; its ironic use of tawāṣaw is the reverse of the section's counsel in patience and mercy.
Faithful people do not take even fathers, sons, brothers, or kin as allies against God; the ayah marks a specific faith boundary within the section's blood ties.
Kin and children cannot benefit one another on the Day of Resurrection; the section's lineage is real, but faith and mercy determine lasting nearness.
God neither begets nor is begotten; the ayah sets a precise divine boundary against the human birth and lineage that opens the section.
God joins hearts that had been enemies until they become brothers; this is a direct communal counterpart to the section's movement from severed kinship to a joined, merciful people.
Abraham asks God to make this town secure and provide its people with fruits, joining the section's town, sheltering neighbors, and relief from hunger.
Abraham asks that he, his son, and their descendants be made submitting community; lineage becomes a chain of shared faith like the section's tawāṣī.
God chooses Adam, Noah, Abraham's family, and Imran's family, giving the section's parentage and descent a prophetic lineage.
The chosen line is described as descendants of one another; this is a direct formulation of lineage continuing through generations.
Zechariah describes his weakened bones and gray hair; this ayah supplies the old age that makes his successor prayer in 19:5 urgent.
Abraham asks that he and his descendants keep prayer, tying offspring to shared faith and practice.
A pregnant divorced woman must be supported until delivery; if she nurses the child, she is paid and the parents consult honorably, joining birth to mutual care.
The next ayah requires each person to provide according to means, completing 65:6's support for the pregnant mother and child.
The command not to kill children from fear of poverty directly reverses the section's threatened lineage and the needy child's vulnerability.
Those who kill their children foolishly and forbid God's provision enact a stark severing of the line the section traces from birth.
The father darkens at news of a daughter and considers hiding her; the ayah shows a family refusing the bond at birth.
He debates keeping the girl in humiliation or burying her in dust; this directly reverses the section's birth and its image of the poor fallen into dust.
The Messenger removes burdens and shackles from people; this is a direct reversal of the section's bound neck and its act of freeing a raqaba.
The ayah asks whether the opponent knows that God sees him, a direct formulation of the section's challenge to the man who thinks nobody saw him.
God joins believers' hearts when no wealth could have united them; this makes the section's joining of separate people into a community concrete.
On the Day the Trumpet is blown, there are no family ties among them; this marks a boundary to the lineage bond the section traces.
On that Day a person flees from his brother, a stark reversal of the section's companion and joined-kin images.
The same person flees from his mother and father, showing descent bonds failing at Judgment.
He flees from his spouse and children, completing the reversal of the section's family and offspring ties.
No close friend asks after another on that Day; this reverses the section's companion as nearness and protection.
People are made to see one another, completing the scene of estranged companions begun in 70:10.
A person would ransom his children from the punishment, making offspring a desperate attempted rescue rather than the section's continuing lineage.
He would also ransom his spouse and brother, extending the failure of close bonds in 70:10.
He would ransom everyone on earth to save himself, completing the breakdown of family and clan solidarity.
Intimate friends become enemies on that Day except the Godwary; the section's companion and mercy roots find their boundary in faith.
The ayah orders help for enslaved people seeking a freedom contract and aid from God's provision, a concrete social form of releasing the bound neck.
The hand chained to the neck is an image of withholding wealth; the ayah warns against stinginess, reversing the section's freeing of a neck and feeding the needy.
Each person comes alone, leaving wealth and intercessors behind; this directly contrasts the section's isolated orphan and its turn toward companions.
The wealthy claimant is told that his possessions will be inherited and that he will come alone; this directly answers the section's boaster, wealth, descendants, and solitude.
Everyone comes to God individually on the Day of Resurrection, a boundary to the section's collective companionship.
A man nearing death must provide a bequest for his wife; this joins the section's waṣiyya (connected speech) to care for a surviving family member.
A child rebukes parents who call him to faith despite their care; this is the opposite of gratitude for parental labor in the section and in 46:15.
The Prophet's gentleness keeps people from dispersing, and he is told to pardon and consult them; this specifies mercy as a force that holds a community together.
The command to cooperate in righteousness and piety gives the section's mutual connection a practical communal form.
Justice must stand even against parents and near relatives; the section's qarāba (kinship) is a bond, but not a license to abandon justice.
Pharaoh promises successful magicians a place among the near ones; this repeated q-r-b wording makes nearness a worldly favor, unlike the section's faith-based closeness.
People fear being snatched from their land if they follow guidance, while God has established a secure sanctuary and provision; this connects the section's town and neighboring life to safety.
Adam and his wife are told to dwell together in the Garden; the section's dictionary form of miskin derives from s-k-n, settling toward a beloved, and this ayah gives that rest a domestic scene.
The same command to dwell in the Garden is addressed to Adam and his wife, repeating the section's s-k-n link between rest and companionship.
Homes are made a sakan (resting place); this Qur'anic sense of the section's miskin root links shelter to the family home.
God sends sakīna into believers' hearts to increase their faith; the section describes faith as calm and the departure of fear.
At the pledge under the tree, God sends tranquility into believers' hearts; this is another communal instance of faith settling fear.
God sends tranquility on the Messenger and believers and binds them to piety, joining faith and calm in a community.
After the believers are shaken in battle, God sends tranquility upon them; this directly illustrates faith's removal of fear.
The disbelievers are described with fetters around their necks, the opposite of the section's freeing a bound neck.
Fetters reach the disbelievers' chins and hold their heads raised; this is a specific reversal of releasing the neck.
The condemned are dragged with shackles around their necks, a direct contrary scene to freeing the neck in the section.
